body.heading: Why a finish line helps
paragraphs: “Study until it's done” has no visible end, so your brain treats it as endless and resists starting. A twenty-five minute sprint is different: the end is close enough to see, and almost anything is bearable for twenty-five minutes.
Set a timer, work on one thing until it rings, then take a real break — stand up, get water, look out of a window. The break is part of the method, not a reward you have to earn.

body.heading: Adjust the length to fit you
paragraphs: Twenty-five minutes is a starting suggestion, not a law. Difficult or boring tasks might suit fifteen; work you enjoy might flow for forty. Experiment for a week and keep the length that leaves you willing to start again tomorrow.
Count sprints, not hours, when you review your day. “I did three sprints” is concrete and encouraging in a way that “I studied for ages” never is.

takeaway: Short, timed sprints make starting easier and stopping guilt-free.
